sectionTitle: Physics — Permanent and induced magnetism, magnetic forces and fields

specStatements.text: The poles of a magnet are the places where the magnetic forces are strongest. When two magnets are brought close together they exert a force on each other. Two like poles repel each other. Two unlike poles attract each other. Attraction and repulsion between two magnetic poles are examples of non-contact force.

A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field. An induced magnet is a material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field. Induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction. When removed from the magnetic field an induced magnet loses most/all of its magnetism quickly.
Students should be able to describe:
• the attraction and repulsion between unlike and like poles for permanent magnets
• the difference between permanent and induced magnets.
The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material (iron, steel, cobalt and nickel) is called the magnetic field.
The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction.
The strength of the magnetic field depends on the distance from the magnet. The field is strongest at the poles of the magnet.

The direction of the magnetic field at any point is given by the direction of the force that would act on another north pole placed at that point. The direction of a magnetic field line is from the north (seeking) pole of a magnet to the south(seeking) pole of the magnet.
A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet. The Earth has a magnetic field. The compass needle points in the direction of the Earth’s magnetic field.
• describe how to plot the magnetic field pattern of a magnet using a compass
• draw the magnetic field pattern of a bar magnet showing how strength and direction change from one point to another
• explain how the behaviour of a magnetic compass is related to evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic.

scopeNotes.statement: a magnetic material (iron, steel, cobalt and nickel)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification names exactly four magnetic materials and nothing here goes beyond that list. Questions asking which objects a magnet attracts use only iron, steel, cobalt and nickel as the magnetic options, with common non-magnetic metals (copper, aluminium, brass, tin) as the contrast. No explanation of why these materials are magnetic is offered - magnetic domains, alloy composition and rare-earth magnets are not part of 4.7.1 and are not introduced.

concepts.definition: A pole is a place on a magnet where the magnetic forces are strongest. A bar magnet has two: a north (seeking) pole and a south (seeking) pole, one at each end.
Like poles are two poles of the same kind (N and N, or S and S) and they repel each other. Unlike poles are one north and one south, and they attract each other.
A force that acts between two objects that are not touching. Attraction and repulsion between two magnetic poles are examples of non-contact force.
A magnet that produces its own magnetic field. It keeps that field whether or not any other magnet is nearby, and it has a fixed north pole and south pole.

A material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field. Induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction, and when the material is removed from the field it loses most or all of its magnetism quickly.
The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material.
A material on which a magnet exerts a force of attraction. The specification names iron, steel, cobalt and nickel.
The strength of the magnetic field depends on the distance from the magnet: it is strongest at the poles and gets weaker as the distance from the magnet increases.
The direction of the magnetic field at any point is the direction of the force that would act on another north pole placed at that point.

A line used to represent a magnetic field. Its direction is from the north (seeking) pole of a magnet to the south (seeking) pole of the magnet, and lines drawn closer together represent a stronger field.
An instrument containing a small bar magnet that is free to turn. The needle lines up with, and points in the direction of, the magnetic field it sits in.
The Earth has a magnetic field, and a compass needle placed away from other magnets points in the direction of the Earth's magnetic field.

A method of finding a field pattern: place a compass near the magnet, mark a dot at each end of the needle, move the compass so its tail sits on the previous head dot, repeat, then join the dots into a line and add an arrow.

A compass points the same way anywhere on the Earth's surface with no magnet nearby. The field must therefore be produced by the Earth itself, which is evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic.

misconceptions.question: Do two magnets always pull towards each other?
misconceptions.correct: No. Two like poles repel each other; two unlike poles attract each other.
misconceptions.misconception: Magnets always stick together, and pushing apart only happens with unusually strong magnets.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Nearly every everyday encounter with a magnet is an attraction - fridge magnets, magnetic catches, picking up paper clips. Repulsion only shows up when a student deliberately turns one magnet round.
misconceptions.correction: Whether the force is a push or a pull depends only on which poles face each other. Like poles (N-N or S-S) repel; unlike poles (N-S) attract. Both are equally ordinary magnetic behaviour.

misconceptions.question: Does a magnet have to touch something to push or pull it?
misconceptions.correct: No. Magnetic attraction and repulsion are non-contact forces, so they act across a gap.
misconceptions.misconception: Nothing happens until the magnets actually touch, because a force needs contact to be passed on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most forces a student meets - pushing a trolley, friction, tension - do need contact, so contact feels like a requirement for any force.
misconceptions.correction: Attraction and repulsion between two magnetic poles are examples of non-contact force. The force is felt through the gap and gets stronger as the gap closes.

misconceptions.question: Where on a bar magnet is the magnetic force strongest?
misconceptions.correct: At the poles, which are at the two ends of the bar.
misconceptions.misconception: The force is strongest in the middle of the bar, because that is where most of the magnet is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason by bulk - more metal in the middle should mean more magnetism - and iron filings pictures are often cropped so the ends are cut off.
misconceptions.correction: The poles of a magnet are the places where the magnetic forces are strongest. Iron filings cluster at the ends of a bar magnet and barely gather at its middle.

misconceptions.question: Does an induced magnet stay magnetic after you take the magnet away?
misconceptions.correct: No. When removed from the magnetic field an induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly.
misconceptions.misconception: Once a paper clip has been magnetised by a magnet it stays a magnet for good.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A chain of paper clips hanging from a magnet looks permanent while the magnet is there, and steel objects can retain a little magnetism, which seems to confirm it.
misconceptions.correction: Induced magnetism depends on the field being present. Take the field away and the induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly, so the chain falls apart.

misconceptions.question: Can an induced magnet repel the magnet that induced it?
misconceptions.correct: No. Induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction.
misconceptions.misconception: If you turn the magnet round, the induced magnet will be pushed away instead of pulled in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer the like-poles-repel rule from two permanent magnets to a case where only one of the objects is a permanent magnet.
misconceptions.correction: The poles induced in the material always line up so that the nearer induced pole is unlike the pole causing it. The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction.

misconceptions.question: Does a magnet attract every metal?
misconceptions.correct: No. It attracts magnetic materials - iron, steel, cobalt and nickel - but not other metals.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything metal will stick to a magnet, because magnetism is a property of metals.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The magnetic objects a student meets at home - tins, screws, fridge doors - are almost all steel, so metal and magnetic look like the same category.
misconceptions.correction: Copper, aluminium, brass, gold and tin are metals but are not magnetic materials. The specification names iron, steel, cobalt and nickel as the magnetic materials.

misconceptions.question: Is a magnetic field only there when something is in it?
misconceptions.correct: No. A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field whether or not anything else is nearby.
misconceptions.misconception: The field only appears when a piece of iron or another magnet is brought close.
misconceptions.whyItArises: You can only detect a field by its effect on something, so the effect and the field get treated as the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: The magnetic field is the region around the magnet where a force would act. It is there all the time; a compass or a piece of iron reveals it rather than creating it.

misconceptions.question: Is the magnetic field the same strength everywhere around a magnet?
misconceptions.correct: No. The strength of the magnetic field depends on the distance from the magnet.
misconceptions.misconception: The field has one fixed strength, and then stops completely at a definite edge.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams show a finite number of field lines ending at the edge of the page, which reads as a boundary where the field switches off.
misconceptions.correction: The field is strongest at the poles and gets steadily weaker with distance from the magnet. It fades away rather than ending at a sharp edge.

misconceptions.question: Which way round are magnetic field lines drawn?
misconceptions.correct: From the north (seeking) pole of a magnet to the south (seeking) pole of the magnet.
misconceptions.misconception: Field lines run from south to north, in the direction the compass needle is pulled towards.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The needle's north end points along the field, but students remember the needle as being pulled to the magnet's north pole and reverse the arrows.
misconceptions.correction: Outside the magnet the arrows go N to S. The direction of the field at any point is the direction of the force on another north pole placed there.

misconceptions.question: Do field lines drawn closer together mean a weaker field?
misconceptions.correct: No. Lines drawn closer together represent a stronger field.
misconceptions.misconception: Lines that are far apart mean the field is stronger, because it reaches further out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word spread gets attached to strength, and the long lines that stretch furthest from the magnet look like the important ones.
misconceptions.correction: The spacing of the lines shows strength: crowded lines near the poles show the strongest field, and widely spaced lines at the sides show a weaker field.

misconceptions.question: What is inside a magnetic compass?
misconceptions.correct: A small bar magnet, free to turn on a pivot.
misconceptions.misconception: The needle is just a light piece of iron that the Earth pulls round.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The needle looks like a plain sliver of metal, and students know that magnets attract iron, so attraction seems enough to explain it.
misconceptions.correction: A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet. Only a magnet has poles that can be pushed one way and pulled the other, which is what turns the needle to a definite direction.

misconceptions.question: Why does a compass needle point north?
misconceptions.correct: Because it lines up with the direction of the Earth's magnetic field.
misconceptions.misconception: It is pulled towards the North Pole because that is the coldest and highest point on the map.
misconceptions.whyItArises: North on a map is drawn at the top, and the North Pole is a single named place, so the needle looks like it is aiming at a location rather than along a field.
misconceptions.correction: The needle is a small bar magnet lining up with the Earth's magnetic field at that point. It reports a field direction, not the position of a place.

misconceptions.question: What does a compass show when there is no magnet nearby?
misconceptions.correct: It still points in the direction of the Earth's magnetic field.
misconceptions.misconception: It swings about randomly, because there is no field to line it up with.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate a field only with a nearby bar magnet, so with no magnet on the bench there seems to be nothing for the needle to respond to.
misconceptions.correction: The Earth has a magnetic field of its own. With no other magnet near, the needle lines up with that field, which is why a compass works out of doors.

misconceptions.question: What does a compass tell us about the inside of the Earth?
misconceptions.correct: That the core of the Earth must be magnetic, because the Earth produces a field of its own.
misconceptions.misconception: The compass points north because of the mass of ice at the North Pole, or because of the atmosphere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for a visible cause at the surface, and the polar ice cap is the most obvious feature at the top of a globe.
misconceptions.correction: A compass points the same way anywhere, with no magnet present, so the field must come from the Earth itself. This is evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic.

misconceptions.question: When you plot a field with a compass, what is the needle doing?
misconceptions.correct: Lining up with the field at that point, so its direction changes as you move it.
misconceptions.misconception: The needle points straight at the nearest pole of the magnet wherever you put it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Near a pole the needle really does aim close to it, and students generalise that one case to every position around the magnet.
misconceptions.correction: The needle takes the direction of the field where it stands. Along the side of a bar magnet that direction is roughly parallel to the magnet, not aimed at a pole.

misconceptions.question: Can the north pole of a magnet attract another magnet?
misconceptions.correct: Yes, if it is facing the south pole of that magnet.
misconceptions.misconception: A single pole by itself fixes the force: a pole is treated as 'an attracting pole' or 'a repelling pole', instead of the force depending on which two poles face each other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students attach attract and repel to a single pole rather than to the pair of poles facing each other.
misconceptions.correction: No pole attracts or repels on its own. It is the combination that matters: like poles repel, unlike poles attract.

misconceptions.question: Which pairs of poles attract: like poles or unlike poles?
misconceptions.correct: Unlike poles attract; like poles repel.
misconceptions.misconception: Poles that are the same are drawn together, and poles that are different push apart.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule is a pair of near-identical sentences that differ by one word, so it is easy to memorise them the wrong way round, and everyday language says like things go together.
misconceptions.correction: Two like poles repel each other. Two unlike poles attract each other. Testing it with two bar magnets, N facing N gives a push and N facing S gives a pull.

misconceptions.question: Does a compass need a current or a coil to work?
misconceptions.correct: No. A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet and needs no electrical parts.
misconceptions.misconception: The needle is turned by a coil of wire inside the case, like an electrical instrument.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Compasses look like meters, and students meet coils and needles together when they later study electromagnetism, so the two get merged.
misconceptions.correction: A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet, free to turn. It has no battery, coil or current; the needle turns because it is itself a magnet sitting in a magnetic field.

misconceptions.question: Paper clips hang in a chain from a magnet. If the magnet is taken away, will the clips push each other apart?
misconceptions.correct: No. The clips were only induced magnets; when the magnet is removed they lose their induced magnetism and simply fall apart.
misconceptions.misconception: The magnet gives every clip the same magnetism, and things carrying the same magnetism push each other apart, like two objects with the same electric charge.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Magnetism is blended with static electricity: students learn that objects charged by contact carry like charges and repel, and transfer that rule to paper clips 'magnetised' by touching the magnet.
misconceptions.correction: Magnetism is not a charge that is shared out. Each clip becomes an induced magnet whose facing poles are opposite, which is why the chain attracts and holds together. When the magnet is removed the induced magnetism largely disappears, so the clips just fall apart - they do not repel each other.

misconceptions.question: Will a copper coin be attracted to a magnet?
misconceptions.correct: No. Copper is not a magnetic material; only iron, steel, cobalt and nickel are attracted to magnets.
misconceptions.misconception: Copper is magnetic, because 'copper' coins stick to a magnet at home.
misconceptions.whyItArises: UK 1p and 2p coins made since 1992 are steel with a thin copper plating, so they really do stick to a magnet; the everyday result is credited to the copper on the outside, while nickel is not recognised as magnetic at all.
misconceptions.correction: The magnetic materials are iron, steel, cobalt and nickel. Pure copper is never attracted to a magnet. Modern 'copper' coins stick only because of the steel underneath the copper coating.

misconceptions.question: A magnet is brought near an unmagnetised iron bar. Which pole appears on the end of the bar nearest the magnet?
misconceptions.correct: The opposite pole to the one facing it, so the induced magnet is always attracted to the magnet.
misconceptions.misconception: The magnet prints its own pole onto the iron: the end of the bar nearest a north pole becomes a north pole, so the magnet and the bar repel.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Induced magnetism is pictured as the magnet copying or stamping its magnetism onto the iron, so the near end is given the same pole as the pole that 'made' it, which would put like poles face to face.
misconceptions.correction: Induction always produces the opposite pole on the near end of the iron: a north pole induces a south pole facing it, and a south pole induces a north pole. That is why induced magnetism always causes attraction, whichever pole of the magnet is used.

mcqs.stem: The north pole of one bar magnet is brought close to the north pole of a second bar magnet. What happens to the magnets?

options.text: They repel each other, because the two poles are alike
options.rationale: Two like poles repel each other, so two north poles push apart.

options.text: They attract, because magnets always pull each other
options.rationale: A student whose experience of magnets is all sticking and lifting assumes every pair of magnets pulls together.

options.text: Nothing happens until the two magnets are touching
options.rationale: Treats the magnetic force as a contact force that only starts once the magnets meet.

options.text: They repel only if one of the magnets is stronger
options.rationale: Gets repulsion right but makes it conditional on strength; the direction depends only on which poles face each other.

mcqs.stem: Two magnets on a bench push each other apart while there is still a 2 cm gap between them. Which statement best describes this force?

options.text: It is a contact force passed through the bench surface
options.rationale: Keeps the idea that a force must be transmitted by something touching, so the bench is recruited as the go-between.

options.text: It is a non-contact force, acting across the air gap
options.rationale: Attraction and repulsion between two magnetic poles are examples of non-contact force, so the force acts over a distance.

options.text: It is a non-contact force only while they move
options.rationale: Confuses the force with the motion it causes; the force acts whether or not the magnets are moving.

options.text: It is a contact force acting through the air
options.rationale: Recognises that something spans the gap but still labels it a contact force, with air treated as the contact.

mcqs.stem: A steel paper clip is held near a strong magnet and becomes magnetic itself. What name is given to the paper clip while it is in the field?

options.text: The clip is a permanent magnet
options.rationale: Treats the clip as having gained a magnetism of its own that it will keep once the magnet is taken away.

options.text: The clip is a non-magnetic metal
options.rationale: Assumes only the original magnet counts as magnetic, so the clip is filed as non-magnetic even though it is steel.

options.text: The clip is an induced magnet
options.rationale: An induced magnet is a material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field.

options.text: The clip is a magnetic pole
options.rationale: Swaps an object for the way a field is represented on a diagram.

mcqs.stem: A chain of paper clips hangs from a bar magnet. The magnet is taken away. What happens to the paper clips?

options.text: They stay in a chain, now permanently magnetic
options.rationale: Treats induced magnetism as something the clips have gained and kept, rather than something the field maintains.

options.text: They push each other apart and scatter widely
options.rationale: Applies the like-poles-repel rule to induced magnets, which always give a force of attraction.

options.text: They stay in a chain for the next few hours
options.rationale: Softer version of the same error: the magnetism is thought to fade slowly rather than go almost at once.

options.text: They lose their magnetism and fall apart
options.rationale: When removed from the magnetic field an induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly.

mcqs.stem: The south pole of one bar magnet is brought near the north pole of another. Which row correctly describes the force?

options.text: Repulsion, because these two poles are different
options.rationale: Reverses the rule, pairing difference with repulsion instead of attraction.

options.text: Attraction, because unlike poles attract each other
options.rationale: Two unlike poles attract each other, and this happens for any pair of N and S poles.

options.text: Attraction, because south poles always attract
options.rationale: Attaches attraction to one pole on its own rather than to the pair of poles facing each other.

options.text: No force at all, as the poles are not alike
options.rationale: Assumes a force only arises between matching poles, so unlike poles are thought to do nothing.

mcqs.stem: A student wants two magnets on trolleys to push apart when released. How should the magnets be arranged?

options.text: With a north pole facing a south pole
options.rationale: Chooses unlike poles, which attract, so the trolleys would run together instead.

options.text: With the two magnets touching end to end
options.rationale: Assumes contact is needed before any force acts, so the trolleys are pushed together first.

options.text: With two north poles facing each other
options.rationale: Two like poles repel each other, so N facing N gives a push apart.

options.text: With one magnet turned on its side
options.rationale: Changes the orientation without controlling which poles face, so the outcome is not decided.

mcqs.stem: Which statement gives a correct difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet?

options.text: An induced magnet keeps its magnetism when it is removed
options.rationale: Exactly reverses the behaviour: an induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly.

options.text: A permanent magnet can only ever attract things
options.rationale: Restricts permanent magnets to attraction, when two like poles of permanent magnets repel.

options.text: An induced magnet has a fixed north pole and south pole
options.rationale: Gives the induced magnet the fixed poles of a permanent magnet; its poles are set by the field it is in.

options.text: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field
options.rationale: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field, while an induced magnet only becomes magnetic in a field.

mcqs.stem: An iron nail is brought near the south pole of a magnet and is pulled in. The magnet is then turned round so the north pole faces the nail. What happens?

options.text: The nail is still pulled towards the magnet
options.rationale: The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction, whichever pole faces it.

options.text: The nail is pushed away, as the pole has changed
options.rationale: Applies the like-poles-repel rule to a nail that has no fixed poles of its own.

options.text: The nail is pushed away only when it is close
options.rationale: Same error, hedged with distance; the force on a magnetic material is attraction at every separation.

options.text: The nail now feels no force from this new pole
options.rationale: Assumes only one pole of a magnet acts on a magnetic material, so the other is thought to do nothing.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is the best definition of a magnetic field?

options.text: The set of lines drawn on a diagram around a bar magnet
options.rationale: Confuses the field with the field lines, which are only a way of representing it on paper.

options.text: The area a magnet covers when it is touching an object
options.rationale: Shrinks the field to the contact area, keeping the idea that magnets act only where they touch.

options.text: The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet
options.rationale: The magnetic field is the region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material.

options.text: The space that fills with force once iron is placed in it
options.rationale: Treats the field as something created by the iron rather than something the magnet produces on its own.

mcqs.stem: A magnet is held over a tray containing a copper coin, a nickel disc, an aluminium strip and a steel screw. Which objects are attracted?

options.text: All four of them, since they are all metals
options.rationale: Treats magnetic and metal as the same category, which is the most common form of this error.

options.text: The copper coin and the steel screw
options.rationale: Keeps steel but swaps in copper, a metal students often expect to be magnetic because it looks like it should be.

options.text: Only the steel screw and nothing else
options.rationale: Recognises steel but misses nickel, which the specification names as a magnetic material.

options.text: Only the nickel disc and the steel screw
options.rationale: Nickel and steel are magnetic materials; copper and aluminium are not.

mcqs.stem: A bar magnet is brought near an unmagnetised iron bar. The magnet is then flipped end for end. Which statement about the force on the iron bar is correct?

options.text: It stays an attraction, whichever pole faces the bar
options.rationale: The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction.

options.text: It now changes from an attraction to a strong repulsion
options.rationale: Carries the two-permanent-magnets rule across to a case where only one object is a magnet.

options.text: It becomes zero, because the two poles now cancel out
options.rationale: Imagines the two poles of the magnet cancelling, when the near pole is the one that acts on the bar.

options.text: It stays a repulsion for each of the two poles
options.rationale: Starts from repulsion, which never happens between a magnet and a magnetic material.

mcqs.stem: Where is the magnetic field of a bar magnet strongest?

options.text: In the middle of the magnet
options.rationale: Reasons by bulk: the middle holds most of the metal, so it is assumed to hold most of the magnetism.

options.text: At the poles of the magnet
options.rationale: The field is strongest at the poles of the magnet.

options.text: Equally strong at every point
options.rationale: Treats the field as having one fixed value everywhere instead of depending on distance and position.

options.text: At the outer ends of the lines
options.rationale: Picks the line that reaches furthest out, mistaking reach for strength.

mcqs.stem: A plotting compass is moved slowly away from the north pole of a bar magnet. What happens to the magnetic field where the compass is?

options.text: It stays exactly the same until a definite edge is reached
options.rationale: Reads the last drawn field line as a boundary where the field stops rather than a fading effect.

options.text: It gets stronger as the compass moves away from the pole
options.rationale: Links strength to the long lines that reach far out, so moving away is thought to strengthen the field.

options.text: It stays the same all the way around the bar magnet
options.rationale: Applies one fixed strength to every point around the magnet, ignoring distance altogether.

options.text: It gets weaker, because the distance from the magnet increases
options.rationale: The strength of the magnetic field depends on the distance from the magnet, so moving away weakens it.

mcqs.stem: Outside a bar magnet, which way do the magnetic field lines point?

options.text: From the north pole to the south pole
options.rationale: The direction of a magnetic field line is from the north (seeking) pole of a magnet to the south (seeking) pole.

options.text: From the south pole across to the north
options.rationale: Reverses the convention, usually by remembering the compass needle as being pulled to the magnet's north pole.

options.text: From each pole in towards the middle
options.rationale: Puts the strongest part of the magnet at its centre, so the lines are drawn heading inwards.

options.text: Always straight out from each pole
options.rationale: Keeps the lines radial and misses the curved path that closes back on the other pole.

mcqs.stem: A compass is placed at a point in the field of a bar magnet. What does the direction the needle's north end points in tell you?

options.text: The straight line from that point to the nearest pole
options.rationale: Generalises what happens right next to a pole to every position around the magnet.

options.text: The direction of the magnetic field at that point
options.rationale: The direction of the field at any point is the direction of the force that would act on another north pole placed at that point.

options.text: The direction the compass would travel if released
options.rationale: Confuses the field direction with a direction of travel; the needle turns, it does not set off.

options.text: The way that a south pole would be pushed there
options.rationale: Uses a south pole as the test pole, which reverses the agreed direction of the field.

mcqs.stem: What is inside a magnetic compass?

options.text: A light piece of iron
options.rationale: Attraction to iron feels like enough to explain the needle, so the needle is taken to be plain iron.

options.text: A coil of thin wire
options.rationale: Imports an electrical component; nothing in a plotting compass carries a current.

options.text: A small bar magnet
options.rationale: A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet, free to turn.

options.text: A drop of liquid metal
options.rationale: Confuses the damping fluid in some compasses with the part that gives the needle its direction.

mcqs.stem: A compass is placed on a bench with no magnets anywhere near it. What does the needle do?

options.text: It settles pointing along the Earth's own magnetic field
options.rationale: The Earth has a magnetic field, and the compass needle points in the direction of the Earth's magnetic field.

options.text: It keeps spinning slowly, as there is no field present
options.rationale: Assumes a field needs a bar magnet nearby, so an empty bench looks like an empty field.

options.text: It points towards the coldest part of the whole room
options.rationale: Treats north as a place with physical properties the needle seeks, rather than a field direction.

options.text: It points straight downwards towards the floor
options.rationale: Confuses the horizontal direction a compass shows with the vertical pull of gravity.

mcqs.stem: A student is plotting the field pattern of a bar magnet using a plotting compass. Which method is correct?

options.text: Slide the compass all the way round the magnet while touching it
options.rationale: Keeps the compass against the magnet, where the needle only reports the nearest pole, so no pattern is built up.

options.text: Mark a dot at each end of the needle, then move the compass on
options.rationale: Marking both ends and moving the compass so its tail sits on the last head dot builds up one field line, which is then joined and given an arrow.

options.text: Draw a straight line from the compass to the nearest pole
options.rationale: Records where the pole is instead of the direction the needle takes at that point.

options.text: Put the compass down and draw round the outside of it
options.rationale: Records the shape of the instrument rather than the direction of the needle inside it.

mcqs.stem: A student draws the field pattern of a bar magnet. Which feature of the drawing shows that the field is stronger near the poles?

options.text: The lines are drawn a long way apart there
options.rationale: Reverses the spacing rule, linking a spread-out pattern with a stronger field.

options.text: The lines are drawn with two arrows on them
options.rationale: Invents a second convention; a field line carries one arrow, which shows direction and not strength.

options.text: The lines are drawn closer together there
options.rationale: Lines drawn closer together represent a stronger field, and they are most crowded at the poles.

options.text: The lines are drawn longer at the poles
options.rationale: Uses the length a line reaches as the measure of strength instead of how crowded the lines are.

mcqs.stem: A compass points the same way on a bench, in a field and out at sea, with no magnets nearby. What does this suggest about the Earth?

options.text: The ice at the North Pole acts like a magnet
options.rationale: Looks for a visible cause at the surface, and polar ice is the obvious feature at the top of a globe.

options.text: The atmosphere is what pulls the needle
options.rationale: Another surface explanation; air is everywhere, which seems to match a field that is everywhere.

options.text: The Earth's gravity is turning the needle
options.rationale: Substitutes the one field students already know for the magnetic field that actually acts on the needle.

options.text: The core of the Earth must be magnetic
options.rationale: A field present everywhere with no magnet nearby must be produced by the Earth itself, which is evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic.
